## business-model / 05_customer-geography.md

_Source: `business-model/05_customer-geography.md`_

# Customer And Geography Map — TSLA

## 1. Customer Map

Tesla does not disclose named, revenue-percentage customer concentration in the filings available in the data pool. Its automotive and services revenue is generated from a large, diffuse base of individual retail vehicle buyers and individual/commercial energy-storage buyers — not from a small number of large institutional accounts. The clearest concentration-relevant disclosure available is a receivables concentration statement, which stands in for a customer-concentration test because Tesla does not publish a percent-of-revenue by customer table.

| Customer Type | Importance (% of revenue if disclosed) | Long-term Contract? (Y/N/Not disclosed) | Evidence | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Individual retail vehicle buyers (Automotive segment) | Majority of revenue — Automotive segment revenue was $69,526M of $94,827M total revenue in FY2025 (73.3%) | N — one-off retail purchase/lease, not a standing contract | [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments sheet, FY2025 (as filed FY25 10-K data)] | Low single-customer risk given diffusion; high sensitivity to aggregate consumer demand, financing rates and incentive policy (demand risk, not concentration risk) |
| Other automobile manufacturers (buyers of automotive regulatory credits) | Small — regulatory credits revenue was $146M in Q2 2026, down 67% y/y, versus $28,236M total Q2 2026 revenue (~0.5%) | N — credit sales are transactional and policy-dependent, not long-term contracts | [FY2025 10-Q (filed Jul-23-2026), MD&A, p. re: Automotive regulatory credits] | Revenue line is shrinking and policy-dependent: "Recent governmental and regulatory actions have restricted certain regulatory credit programs tied to our products" [FY2025 10-Q, MD&A] |
| Commercial / utility / data-center energy-storage customers (Energy Generation and Storage segment) | Energy segment revenue was $12,771M in FY2025 (13.5% of total) and $3,139M in Q2 2026; management describes deployments as "lumpy" and "tied to customer time lines" | Not disclosed at the individual-customer level; some framework agreements disclosed (e.g., SPIE multi-year BESS framework agreement across France/Belgium/Netherlands, extendable to Poland/Germany) | [Key Developments, Client Announcement, 2025-12-15]; [Q2 2026 earnings call, Jul-22-2026, CFO prepared remarks] | Segment-level lumpiness tied to a handful of large individual deployments (utility/data-center scale) is a real risk even though no single customer's revenue share is disclosed |
| Named individual large counterparties in CIQ relationship data (banks, auto retailers, energy developers, SpaceX/X.AI, Rivian, etc.) | Not disclosed as % of revenue — these are relationship-type records (borrower, lessee, distributor, licensee), not revenue-ranked customers | Not disclosed | [CIQ Customers export, Tesla Inc NasdaqGS TSLA Customers.xls] | None quantifiable; useful only as a qualitative list of counterparties, not a concentration signal |

Not proven from available data: a named "Customer A accounts for X%" disclosure. Tesla's business model (millions of individual vehicle and product buyers) makes single-customer concentration structurally unlikely, and the only quantitative concentration test the filings provide (receivables, not revenue) confirms this — see Section 3.

## 2. Geography Map

Tesla reports revenue by three geographic buckets: United States, China, and Other International (Europe, rest of Asia-Pacific, and rest of world combined) [FY2025 10-Q (filed Jul-23-2026), Note 14 — Segment Reporting and Information about Geographic Areas; CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments sheet].

| Geography | % of Revenue | Trend (Growing / Stable / Declining / Unknown) | Evidence | Risk |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| United States | 50.2% (FY2025: $47,627M of $94,827M); 47.2% in H1 2026 ($23,885M of $50,623M) | Growing on a full-year basis (48.8% in FY2024 → 50.2% in FY2025); roughly stable in H1 2026 vs FY2025 | [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments sheet, FY2024–FY2025]; [FY2025 10-Q, Note 14, six months ended Jun-30-2026 vs Jun-30-2025] | Largest single-country exposure; sensitive to US interest rates (loan/lease subvention costs), US vehicle-emission-credit policy, and US import tariffs |
| China | 22.1% (FY2025: $20,962M of $94,827M); 17.5% in H1 2026 ($8,859M of $50,623M) | Declining share (21.4% FY2024 → 22.1% FY2025 → 17.5% H1 2026) | [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments sheet]; [FY2025 10-Q, Note 14] | Geopolitical, tariff, and local-competition risk (BYD and other domestic EV makers); China is also a manufacturing/export base (Gigafactory Shanghai), so the country carries both revenue and asset exposure |
| Other International (Europe, APAC ex-China, rest of world) | 27.7% (FY2025: $26,238M of $94,827M); 35.3% in H1 2026 ($17,879M of $50,623M) | Growing sharply in H1 2026 (27.7% FY2025 → 35.3% H1 2026); management cited sequential Q2-2026 delivery growth of 27% (APAC) and 12% (EMEA) | [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments sheet]; [FY2025 10-Q, Note 14]; [Q2 2026 earnings call, Jul-22-2026, CFO prepared remarks] | Aggregated bucket masks country-level concentration within Europe/RoW — filings do not break this out further |

Long-lived assets follow a similar US-weighted pattern: United States $35,847M at Dec-31-2025 versus Other International $9,400M (a roughly 79%/21% split); at Jun-30-2026, United States $42,213M versus Other International $9,552M (about 82%/18%) [FY2025 10-Q, Note 14]. Production and physical-asset concentration in the US is even higher than the revenue split, which increases the exposure of a US-specific shock (tariff, regulation, natural disaster) relative to a pure revenue read.

Geographic shares sum to ~100% in each period shown; "Other International" is a single combined bucket that the filings do not split further by country.

## 3. Concentration Flags

| Concentration Flag | Triggered (Y/N) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| One customer >20% of revenue | N | No customer is named with a revenue percentage in the filings. The closest available quantitative test — accounts-receivable concentration — shows: "As of June 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, no entity represented 10% or more of our total receivables balance." [FY2025 10-Q, Note — Concentration of Risk]. This is a receivables test, not a revenue test, but it is the only concentration figure Tesla discloses and it is well under 20%. |
| Top 3 customers >40% of revenue | N | Not disclosed, and structurally implausible given a retail-diffuse buyer base across automotive and most of energy storage; no evidence of institutional buyer concentration at this scale. |
| One geography >50% of revenue | Y | United States was 50.2% of FY2025 revenue ($47,627M of $94,827M) [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments sheet, FY2025]. On a trailing-six-month basis (H1 2026) the US share was 47.2%, just under the 50% line [FY2025 10-Q, Note 14], so the trigger is annual-period-dependent and sits right at the threshold rather than deep past it. |
| One customer or geography >30% with no long-term contract disclosed | Y | United States revenue (>30% in every period shown) is generated through one-off retail vehicle sales and services, not long-term supply or offtake contracts [FY2025 10-Q, Note 14; CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments sheet]. This reflects organic consumer-demand dependency on the home market, not a counterparty-contract risk — there is no single anchor customer behind the US number. |

## 4. Read

Tesla's concentration risk sits almost entirely on the geography side, not the customer side: the filings show no entity holding 10% or more of receivables [FY2025 10-Q, Note — Concentration of Risk], and the business model (millions of individual buyers) makes customer concentration structurally unlikely. Geographically, the United States crossed 50% of FY2025 revenue [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments sheet] and carries an even larger share of long-lived assets (~79–82%) [FY2025 10-Q, Note 14], while China's revenue share fell from about 22% (FY2025) to about 17.5% (H1 2026) as "Other International" (Europe/APAC ex-China/RoW) grew to over a third of revenue [FY2025 10-Q, Note 14; Q2 2026 earnings call]. None of this geographic revenue is secured by long-term contracts — it is organic, demand-driven, and swings with regional deliveries, incentives, and tariffs each quarter. The single biggest dependency the synthesizer should carry forward: Tesla now earns roughly half its revenue and over three-quarters of its long-lived assets in one country (the United States), with no contractual protection against a US-specific demand, tariff, or policy shock.

## business-model / 06_value-chain.md

# Value Chain Position — TSLA

## 1. Stages Occupied

| Value Chain Stage | Company Role (1 sentence) | Bargaining Power vs Upstream | Bargaining Power vs Downstream | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Raw material / component processor | Tesla buys globally-traded battery-grade lithium, nickel, steel, aluminum, and many components (including from single-source suppliers), while increasingly making its own cathode material, refined lithium, and battery cells in-house. | Weak | Strong (internal transfer to its own factories) | "We are dependent on our suppliers, including single source suppliers, and the inability of these suppliers to deliver necessary components... could have a material adverse effect on our business" [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Notes, Supply Risk]; "Commodity price increases and interest rate changes all continue to add to our costs" [Q2 FY2026 transcript, prepared remarks]; "we started production with the lithium refinery, the cathode refinery... we're scaling up battery cell production" [Q2 FY2026 transcript, prepared remarks] |
| Manufacturer / assembler (Gigafactories) | Owns and runs its own vehicle and Megapack/Powerwall assembly plants (Fremont, Austin, Berlin, Shanghai, Nevada, Lathrop, and a Megafactory under construction near Houston) rather than contract-manufacturing. | Mid | Strong (owns the distribution channel that follows) | "additional localized procurement and manufacturing are key to our vehicles' affordability" [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A]; Megafactory build-out in Shanghai, Lathrop, and near Houston [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A, "Energy Generation and Storage Demand, Production and Deployment"] |
| Distributor / retailer (direct-to-consumer) | Sells and services vehicles through its own stores, website, delivery network, and company-run service centers — no independent franchised dealer network sits between Tesla and the buyer. | Strong (same company as manufacturing) | Mid | "Tesla... sells cars straight to buyers — through its own stores, website, and delivery network — rather than through independent franchised dealers" [Business identity, §1, citing Tesla Inc NasdaqGS TSLA Public Company Profile.rtf]; automotive gross margin fell from 18.2% (FY2023) to 16.2% (FY2025) to 16.9% GAAP / 16.3% ex-credits (Q2 FY2026) despite management describing per-unit cost as "relatively consistent" [03_segment-map.md; Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] |
| Platform / infrastructure and software provider | Sells access to its own proprietary Supercharger network to rival automakers under the NACS standard, and sells a paid FSD (Supervised) driver-assist subscription directly to vehicle buyers. | Strong (fully owned, no third-party IP dependency) | Strong | "other automotive manufacturers have announced their adoption of NACS and agreements with us to utilize our Superchargers" [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A]; "In Q2, we had in North America, about 55% of our deliveries had FSD subscription at the time of delivery" [Q2 FY2026 transcript, prepared remarks] |
| Regulatory-credit seller | Sells automotive regulatory (emissions/ZEV) credits to other automakers that need them to meet government mandates — a near-pure-margin, policy-created revenue line, not a negotiated commercial sale. | N/A (byproduct of the automotive stage; no distinct input) | Weak | "Automotive regulatory credits revenue decreased $293 million, or 67%, in the three months ended June 30, 2026... impacted by changes in regulation" and "Recent governmental and regulatory actions have restricted certain regulatory credit programs tied to our products" [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] |

Bargaining power bands:
- **Strong:** Company sets price, dictates terms, has alternatives
- **Mid:** Negotiated outcomes, no extreme leverage either way
- **Weak:** Price-taker, terms imposed, few alternatives

## 2. Input Cost Pass-Through

Tesla's ability to pass rising input costs to customers is partial and lossy, not automatic. On the automotive side, management credits "effective pricing and cost management" for holding gross margin "approximately flat" quarter-on-quarter once one-off items are stripped out [Q2 FY2026 transcript, prepared remarks], but the multi-year trend argues the other way: GAAP automotive gross margin fell from 18.2% in FY2023 to 16.2% in FY2025 [03_segment-map.md, citing CIQ Financials_Annual export] even as per-unit cost stayed "relatively consistent" [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] — the gap was closed mostly by regulatory-credit contribution and cost cuts, not by raising sticker prices. Tariff cost relief has shown up as one-off, laggy recognitions rather than a structural escalator: Tesla booked "more than $250 million from certain tariffs which we paid in prior quarters" as an energy-segment benefit in Q1 FY2026 that then "did not repeat" in Q2 [Q1 FY2026 transcript, prepared remarks; Q2 FY2026 transcript, prepared remarks]. There is no disclosed contractual pass-through clause (escalator or indexed pricing) for retail vehicle sales in this pool — automotive sales are one-off retail transactions, not standing supply contracts [05_customer-geography.md]. On the energy side, management is explicit that trying to pass tariff-driven battery-cell cost increases through to customers is self-defeating: "import tariffs by the US government and the provisions of the OBBBA could significantly increase battery cell expenses and impact costs for our consumers, negatively impacting consumer demand" [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A]. Not proven from available data: any numeric lag (in days or quarters) between an input cost rise and a matching price change, beyond the tariff-recognition timing above.

**Supplier / input concentration (quantify).** The filings do not quantify supplier concentration — there is no disclosed percentage of cost of revenue or purchases tied to the largest supplier or the top three suppliers, and no dollar figure attached to the single-source dependency. The 10-Q states only, in general terms, that Tesla is "dependent on our suppliers, including single source suppliers," without naming them or sizing the exposure [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Notes, Supply Risk]. The one input concentration that is specifically named and material is geographic rather than a single company: for the Energy Generation and Storage segment, "most of the battery cells are procured from China," and management flags this as the reason "tariffs in this business can have outsized impacts" [Q1 FY2026 transcript, prepared remarks]. That segment was 13.5% of FY2025 revenue but 22.2% of FY2025 gross profit and growing [03_segment-map.md] — so a China-battery-cell single-country dependency sits directly inside Tesla's fastest-improving profit pool. Not proven from available data: the dollar or percentage split of Tesla's total raw-material or component purchases between in-house-produced (lithium, cathode, cells) and externally-sourced inputs.

## 3. Customer Pricing Power

Tesla has not demonstrated an ability to raise prices without losing volume in the periods covered by this pool. No explicit sticker-price increase is documented in the last 24 months; instead, the automotive average selling price moved on "sales mix and a positive impact from the weakening of the United States dollar... and an increase from higher revenue from FSD (Supervised) subscriptions" [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] — mix, currency, and software attach, not a price hike on the core vehicle. Automotive gross margin has trended down for three straight years (18.2% FY2023 → 16.9% FY2024 → 16.2% FY2025) [03_segment-map.md] even as Q2 FY2026 revenue growth was explicitly volume-led ("an increase of approximately 25% in cash deliveries") [Business identity, §4, citing Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] — consistent with a company competing on volume, not price, against BYD and legacy-OEM EVs. On the energy side, management states plainly that "ASPs for industrial storage is coming down amidst growing competition" [Q2 FY2026 transcript, prepared remarks], and Q2 FY2026 energy gross margin fell sharply from 30.3% to 20.4% on "a decrease in average selling price per Megapack unit" [Business identity, §2, citing Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A]. The one clear pricing-power exception is software, not hardware: about 55% of North America deliveries carried a paid FSD (Supervised) subscription at the time of delivery in Q2 FY2026 [Q2 FY2026 transcript, prepared remarks], but that sits on top of a base vehicle price that is itself under competitive pressure, not evidence that Tesla can move the core product's price.

## 4. Economic Control Verdict

**Mixed.** Tesla controls the middle of its value chain — it owns its factories, bypasses the independent dealer network that squeezes most automakers, and increasingly monetizes proprietary infrastructure and software (Supercharger access sold to rival OEMs, paid FSD subscriptions) on terms it sets [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A; Q2 FY2026 transcript, prepared remarks]. But it is a price-taker on globally traded battery-grade commodities and disclosed single-source components upstream [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Notes, Supply Risk], and it cannot raise prices to end customers without losing volume on either the automotive side (three years of margin decline despite flat unit cost) or the energy side ("ASPs for industrial storage is coming down amidst growing competition") [03_segment-map.md; Q2 FY2026 transcript, prepared remarks]. The near-pure-margin regulatory-credit revenue that has historically cushioned automotive margin is set entirely by government policy, not by negotiation, and it fell 67% year-on-year in Q2 FY2026 [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A].

## 5. The Single Biggest Bargaining Risk

The Energy segment's reliance on China-sourced battery cells under an escalating US tariff and OBBBA regime is the relationship most likely to hurt Tesla if it worsens — it raises input cost in the segment where gross profit has grown fastest, and management itself says passing that cost to customers would cut demand rather than protect margin [Q1 FY2026 transcript, prepared remarks; Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A].

## business-model / 07_business-quality.md

# Business Quality — TSLA

**Sector overlay:** No sector overlay for vertically-integrated EV manufacturer — generic 11-factor scoring applies. `frameworks/SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md` has no row for "auto OEM" / "EV manufacturer"; `02_business-identity.md` §3a already confirmed this and applied the sheet's own "Generic operating company (default)" grammar (volume, price/mix, utilization, order book, segment mix, working-capital cycle) [`02_business-identity.md`, §3a]. That generic grammar is used below.

## 1. Quality Factor Table

| Quality Factor | Score /100 | Evidence | Comment |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pricing power *(higher = better)* | 35 | Consolidated gross margin fell from 25.6% (FY2022) to 18.2% (FY2023), 17.9% (FY2024), 18.0% (FY2025) [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Ratios tab, "Gross Margin %" row]; automotive segment gross margin (ex-regulatory-credits) was 16.3% in Q2 FY2026, down from a multi-year high above 25% [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A; `03_segment-map.md` §1]; Automotive ASP moves were "primarily driven by sales mix" and FX, not list-price increases [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] | Volume-led growth (18% higher deliveries H1 FY2026) has repeatedly come with margin give-back, not price increases held; the near-pure-margin regulatory-credit line — Tesla's best pricing-power proxy — has itself fallen 67% YoY under policy pressure [`10_external-dependency.md` §1], which is a headwind, not an offset |
| Repeat / recurring revenue *(higher = better)* | 35 | Automotive one-off vehicle sales are 73.3% of FY2025 revenue [`05_customer-geography.md` §1]; "Services and other" (used cars, paid Supercharging, FSD subscriptions, insurance) — the closest thing to recurring, usage-based revenue — is 13.2% of FY2025 revenue ($12,530M of $94,827M), growing 46–50% YoY in H1 FY2026 [`03_segment-map.md` §1] | The recurring tail is real and the fastest-growing line, but it is still a minority of revenue with no full-year margin disclosure [`03_segment-map.md` §3]; the core business is transactional retail vehicle sale, not subscription or contracted revenue |
| Customer stickiness *(higher = better)* | 32 | Vehicle purchases/leases are "one-off retail purchase/lease, not a standing contract" [`05_customer-geography.md` §1]; no long-term contracts disclosed with any customer segment, including Energy's utility/commercial buyers beyond isolated framework agreements (e.g. SPIE BESS) [`05_customer-geography.md` §1] | Some ecosystem lock-in exists (Supercharger network, paid FSD subscription retention) but none of it is quantified in the pool; the dominant automotive customer relationship is a single transaction with no contractual renewal mechanism |
| Margin stability *(higher = better)* | 22 | Operating (EBIT) margin collapsed from 16.8% (FY2022) to 9.2% (FY2023), 7.8% (FY2024), 4.6% (FY2025), 4.1% (LTM Jun-2026) [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Ratios tab, "EBIT Margin %" row]; automotive segment gross margin fell every year shown, 18.2% (FY2023) → 16.9% (FY2024) → 16.2% (FY2025) [`03_segment-map.md` §1]; Energy segment margin swung from 39.5% (Q1 FY2026) to 20.4% (Q2 FY2026) in one quarter [`03_segment-map.md` §1] | This is the weakest row in the table: operating margin has fallen every year for three straight years and roughly quartered off its FY2022 peak — a durable, structural compression, not a one-quarter blip |
| Capital intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 28 | Capital expenditure was $8,527M in FY2025 and $12,923M LTM Jun-2026 (revised to include energy-storage capex from Q1 FY2025 onward) against $94,827M FY2025 revenue (~9% of revenue) and $103,619M LTM revenue (~12.5%) [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Cash Flow tab, "Capital Expenditure" row; `03_segment-map.md` §4 footnote]; segment map rates both Automotive and Energy "Capital Intensity: High" (multiple Gigafactories/Megafactories, new tooling for Cybercab/Semi/Optimus, capex not split by segment) [`03_segment-map.md` §1] | Vertically-integrated manufacturing (own cell production, cathode material, lithium refining in Texas [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A]) means the capital bill keeps growing even as the core automotive margin it is meant to protect keeps falling |
| Competitive intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 28 | 10-Q explicitly warns "as additional competitors enter the marketplace ... we will have to adjust and continue to execute well to maintain our momentum" [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A]; automotive gross margin compression across FY2023–FY2025 coincides with a rising number of global EV entrants (BYD and other domestic Chinese makers named as a China-market risk) [`05_customer-geography.md` §2] | Falling core-segment margin in a growing-revenue environment is itself evidence of price/margin competition, not just cost inflation — management's own cost-reduction language ("competitively price our vehicles") concedes the price side of the fight [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] |
| Industry rate-of-change / disruption risk *(low rate-of-change = high score)* | 30 | Filing itself calls the industry "cyclical" and sensitive to "shifting consumer trends" and new entrants [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A]; simultaneously the company is pivoting its own growth story toward robotaxi/FSD and Optimus humanoid robots — technologies with no disclosed revenue line and gated by unresolved, state-by-state regulation ("There seems to be some evolving regulations at the state level ... there is not a federal framework") [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A; `10_external-dependency.md` §1] | The competitive set for both EVs (Chinese entrants, legacy-OEM EV pushes, battery-chemistry shifts) and autonomous driving/robotics is genuinely unsettled — this is the CLAUDE.md §24 Filter 5 "early-stage EV / robotaxi" case in substance, not just in label |
| Regulatory dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 28 | Automotive regulatory-credit revenue fell 67% YoY in Q2 FY2026 "impacted by ... changes in regulation" and explicit "governmental and regulatory actions" restricting the program [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A]; OBBBA and tariff policy "could significantly increase battery cell expenses" for the energy business [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A]; robotaxi scale-up is gated by unresolved state-level safety regulation [`10_external-dependency.md` §1] | `10_external-dependency.md` §4 independently scored government-policy/regulation dependence "High" — three separate regulatory levers (credits, tariffs, robotaxi rules) hit results or the growth story directly, none of them controlled by Tesla |
| Commodity dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 48 | "Commodity price increases and interest rate changes all continue to add to our costs" [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks]; raw-materials inventory rose from $4.52bn (Dec-31-2025) to $4.70bn (Jun-30-2026) [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Note — Inventory]; `10_external-dependency.md` §1 rates commodity-price dependence "Mid" | Vertical integration into cathode material and lithium refining (Texas ramp under way, H1 FY2026) [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] is a real, partial offset — this keeps the score at the middle of the band rather than the low end reserved for a pure price-taker |
| Cyclicality *(low cyclicality = high score)* | 28 | The 10-Q states plainly the company "operate[s] in a cyclical industry that is sensitive to shifting consumer trends ... inflationary pressures, rising energy prices, interest rate fluctuations" [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A]; automotive-sales revenue was down 11% YoY in Q4 FY2025 then up 23–27% YoY in Q1–Q2 FY2026 [`03_segment-map.md` §1]; Return on Capital swung from 18.6% (FY2022 peak) to 8.9% (FY2023), 6.0% (FY2024), 2.9% (FY2025), 2.75% (LTM) [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Ratios tab, "Return on Capital %" row] | Both the qualitative filing language and the hard numbers (delivery swings, ROIC collapse) agree — this is a demand-cyclical, capital-intensive manufacturer, not a steady-state compounder |
| Disclosure quality *(higher = better)* | 55 | Segment note discloses revenue, cost of revenue, and gross profit only — no segment operating expense, operating income, or net income, so no outside party can compute true segment ROIC [`03_segment-map.md` §3]; no numeric factory-utilization rate or vehicle order-backlog disclosed [`02_business-identity.md` §3a]; Robotaxi/Optimus/FSD carry no separate revenue-line disclosure at all [`03_segment-map.md` §3]; original standalone FY2025 10-K (Item 8 financials, full risk-factor text) is absent from the pool — only the Part III-only 10-K/A amendment and CIQ exports stand in [`00_data-triage.md` §3] | Quantitative disclosure (revenue, margin, cash flow, FX sensitivity) is timely and detailed at the consolidated level, and no disqualifying integrity or auditor red flag was found [`01_disqualifier-scan.md`]; the gap is depth on the two things that matter most to a buyer today — true segment profitability and the size of the AI/robotics bet — not basic transparency |

Bands: 0–20 Very weak · 21–40 Weak · 41–60 Mixed/Average · 61–80 Strong · 81–100 Very strong.

## 2. Aggregate Quality Score

**Aggregate: 33/100 (Weak).**

Weights used: Margin stability 15%, Competitive intensity 15%, Industry rate-of-change 15%, Cyclicality 10%, Regulatory dependence 10%, Pricing power 10%, Capital intensity 8%, Recurring revenue 7%, Customer stickiness 5%, Commodity dependence 3%, Disclosure quality 2%. The weighted read comes to ≈30, rounded up slightly to 33 to reflect the partial, evidenced offsets noted in each row's Comment column (vertical integration, a growing recurring-revenue tail, clean audit history). The lowest row (Margin stability, 22) and second-lowest cluster (Capital intensity / Competitive intensity / Regulatory dependence / Cyclicality, all 28) anchor the aggregate — 33 sits within 11 points of the second-lowest score, well inside the ~20-point band-anchor ceiling (28 + 20 = 48 max). Margin stability, competitive intensity, cyclicality, and rate-of-change dominate this read because they describe the same underlying fact from four angles: a capital-intensive, demand-cyclical manufacturer whose core-segment margin has fallen every year for three straight years while new competitors enter. Disclosure quality and commodity dependence are secondary and do not rescue the score.

## 3. Strongest Factor & Weakest Factor

| | Factor | Score | Why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Strongest | Disclosure quality | 55 | Detailed, timely quantitative disclosure at the consolidated level (revenue, margin, cash flow, FX sensitivity) with a clean audit history and no disqualifier trigger [`01_disqualifier-scan.md`], even though segment-level profitability and the AI/robotics bet remain undisclosed |
| Weakest | Margin stability | 22 | Operating margin fell every year for three straight years — 16.8% (FY2022) → 9.2% (FY2023) → 7.8% (FY2024) → 4.6% (FY2025) → 4.1% (LTM) [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Ratios tab] — a structural, multi-year compression, not a one-off |

## 4. Read

Tesla is a capital-intensive, demand-cyclical vehicle manufacturer with a smaller, faster-growing grid-battery business bolted on, plus an unmonetized bet on autonomous driving and robotics — not a durable compounder in its current, disclosed form. Return on capital collapsed from an 18.6% cyclical peak in FY2022 to 2.9% in FY2025 and 2.75% LTM [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Ratios tab, "Return on Capital %"]; that FY2022 peak was itself a cyclical high (pandemic-era supply shortage plus a near-monopoly EV position), not a through-cycle level, so today's ~3% figure is the more honest read of what this business earns on capital absent another unusual demand spike — and it sits well below any reasonable cost of capital. The single quality factor a buyer should watch over the next 24 months is margin stability: whether automotive gross margin (16.2% FY2025, 16.3% Q2 FY2026 ex-credits) stabilizes as the shrinking regulatory-credit line fully runs off, or keeps falling as EV competition intensifies and the robotaxi/Optimus story — still a zero-revenue-line item in the segment disclosure — consumes capital without a matching return. Because the industry rate-of-change / disruption-risk row scored 30 (≤40), this thesis is flagged explicitly as closer to a sector / technology-cycle bet (EV competitive dynamics plus an unresolved autonomous-driving regulatory race) than a durable compounder.

RF-BQ-005 (fast-changing industry: rate-of-change ≤40)

## business-model / 08_competitive-map.md

_Source: `business-model/08_competitive-map.md`_

# Competitive Map — TSLA

Both required upstream inputs are present: `02_business-identity.md` and `03_segment-map.md`.

## 1. Dominant Segment

Automotive is Tesla's dominant segment — 86.5% of FY2025 revenue and 77.7% of FY2025 gross profit (gross-profit basis only; Tesla does not allocate operating expenses by segment) [`CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments tab, FY2025`; `FY26 Q2 10-Q, Note 14`], restated from `03_segment-map.md` §2.

## 2. Named Competitors

A hard limitation up front: the data pool does not contain Tesla's own Item 1A "Risk Factors" / "Competition" narrative — only a Part III-only Form 10-K/A amendment is present for FY2025, and neither the Q1 FY2026 nor Q2 FY2026 earnings-call transcripts in this pool name a specific competitor by name (management discusses "additional competitors" generically) [`Tesla_Inc_-_Form_10-KA(Apr-30-2026)`; `Tesla, Inc., Q1/Q2 FY2026 Earnings Call transcripts`]. The competitor set below is therefore built from the Capital IQ peer-comp export in the data pool (a Tier-5 vendor source, built specifically for TSLA using CIQ's own relevancy scoring) plus one competitor confirmed only through dated trade press, since it does not appear anywhere in the pool.

### Competitor A — BYD Company Limited

- **Ticker / listing:** HKEX:1211 / SZSE:002594 (not in the data pool's CIQ comp set)
- **Where they compete:** Battery-electric and plug-in-hybrid passenger vehicles globally, directly overlapping Tesla's Automotive segment in China, Europe, and emerging markets.
- **Scale:** FY2025 revenue of roughly $116 billion (USD-converted), above Tesla's LTM total revenue of $103,619 million [`Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Financial Data tab, LTM as of 2026-07-24`]; BYD delivered about 2.26 million battery-electric vehicles in 2025 versus Tesla's 1.64 million deliveries, a roughly 620,000-unit gap [Web: goodcarbadcar.net, "BYD Beat Tesla in Revenue — But Profits Fell 19% in 2025," pub. 2026-04-03, unverified — not in the data pool].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** FY2025 net profit approximately $4.7 billion on ~$116 billion revenue — a net margin of roughly 4.0% — down 19% year-on-year as a domestic Chinese price war compressed margins, "the company's first annual profit drop since 2021" [Web: goodcarbadcar.net, pub. 2026-04-03, unverified]. For comparison, Tesla's own LTM net-income margin is 3.67% and LTM return on capital is 2.75% [`Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics tab`; `Tesla Inc NasdaqGS TSLA Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab, LTM Jun-30-2026`]. ROIC/ROE for BYD specifically is not disclosed anywhere in this data pool — the ~4.0% net margin above is a web-derived estimate, not an audited figure, and should not be read as precise.
- **Source named in:** Not named in any Tesla filing or transcript in this pool. Named in dated industry trade press as the company that overtook Tesla as the world's top BEV seller in 2025 [Web: CnEVPost, "BYD leads global BEV market with 15.4% share in Q3," pub. 2025-11-24, unverified; Web: autovistagroup/visualcapitalist EV market-share summaries, 2026, unverified].
- **One-line read:** Higher volume, roughly comparable net margin, but the company that took the "world's top EV seller by volume" title away from Tesla in calendar 2025 — not proven from Tesla's own filings, since Tesla's pool documents never name BYD.

### Competitor B — Ford Motor Company

- **Ticker / listing:** NYSE:F
- **Where they compete:** US and global light-vehicle manufacturer with a growing EV lineup (Mustang Mach-E, F-150 Lightning), competing with Tesla's Automotive segment mainly in North America [`Company Comparable Analysis Tesla Inc .xls, Business Description tab`].
- **Scale:** LTM total revenue $189,861 million (LTM filing date 2026-04-30), about 1.83x Tesla's LTM revenue of $103,619 million [`Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Financial Data tab`].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** LTM gross margin 7.1%, LTM EBITDA margin 4.0%, LTM EBIT margin 0.8%, LTM net-income margin −3.2% (net loss on a trailing basis), LTM total debt/capital 81.0% [`Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics tab`]. ROIC/ROE for Ford specifically: not disclosed in this data pool.
- **Source named in:** `Company Comparable Analysis Tesla Inc .xls` — Capital IQ's own peer-comp set built for TSLA, sorted by "S&P Capital IQ's proprietary relevancy score" [Trading Multiples tab, Financial Data tab, Operating Statistics tab, Business Description tab].
- **One-line read:** Far larger revenue base built on legacy internal-combustion volume, but with gross, EBITDA, and net margins well below Tesla's on every line disclosed in this pool.

### Competitor C — General Motors Company

- **Ticker / listing:** NYSE:GM
- **Where they compete:** US and global light-vehicle manufacturer (Chevrolet, Cadillac, GMC, Buick) with its own EV lineup and a large China joint-venture presence, competing with Tesla's Automotive segment in North America and China [`Company Comparable Analysis Tesla Inc .xls, Business Description tab`].
- **Scale:** LTM total revenue $185,528 million (LTM filing date 2026-07-21), about 1.79x Tesla's LTM revenue [`Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Financial Data tab`].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** LTM gross margin 10.2%, LTM EBITDA margin 8.9%, LTM EBIT margin 5.5%, LTM net-income margin 1.05%, LTM total debt/capital 66.9% [`Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics tab`]. ROIC/ROE for GM specifically: not disclosed in this data pool.
- **Source named in:** Same `Company Comparable Analysis Tesla Inc .xls` CIQ peer-comp export.
- **One-line read:** Profitable at the operating line, unlike Ford, but still a fraction of Tesla's gross margin and net margin, carrying much more balance-sheet leverage (67% debt/capital vs. Tesla's 15.5%) [`Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics tab`; `Tesla Inc NasdaqGS TSLA Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab`].

## 3. Competitive Position

**Losing** global battery-electric-vehicle volume share to BYD on a full calendar-year 2025 basis: BYD held roughly 12.1% of the global BEV market in 2025 versus Tesla's 8.8% (Volkswagen third at 5.2%), and BYD's battery-electric volume (2.26 million units) grew 28% year-on-year while Tesla's global deliveries (1.64 million) fell from the prior year [Web: autovistagroup/visualcapitalist EV market-share summaries, 2026, unverified — not in the data pool]. That said, Tesla's own most recent quarters show a different, more recent trend: automotive-sales revenue was down 11% year-on-year in Q4 FY2025 but up 23–27% year-on-year in Q1–Q2 FY2026 [`03_segment-map.md` §1, citing `FY26 Q2 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A`]. The data pool does not disclose Tesla's own global market-share trend directly, so the full-year-2025 share loss and the early-2026 revenue rebound are the two best available reads and they point in different directions — the rebound could reflect regained share, an industry-wide demand recovery, or both; it is not proven from available data which.

## 4. Competitive Shape

**Fragmented.** No single manufacturer holds anywhere near a dominant share of the global BEV market: BYD leads at roughly 12.1%, Tesla second at 8.8%, Volkswagen third at 5.2% — the top three combine for only about 26% of the market, with the balance split across a long tail of Chinese domestic brands (Geely, SAIC, Xiaomi, Li Auto, NIO, XPeng, Wuling — none named in this data pool) and legacy Western/Japanese/Korean OEMs building out competing EV lineups, several of which appear in Tesla's own Capital IQ peer-comp set: Ford, General Motors, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Renault, Kia, Stellantis, plus EV pure-plays Rivian and Lucid [Web: autovistagroup/visualcapitalist EV market-share summaries, 2026, unverified; `Company Comparable Analysis Tesla Inc .xls, Business Description tab`]. This is not a 2–4 firm oligopoly and not a consolidated market — it is a large field of scaled competitors with no HHI concentration data available in this pool to quantify precisely.

## 5. Caveat

The data pool's own Tesla documents do not name specific competitors: the only Form 10-K present is a Part III-only amendment (`Tesla_Inc_-_Form_10-KA(Apr-30-2026)`), which lacks the Item 1A "Risk Factors" / "Competition" section a full annual filing would carry, and neither in-pool earnings-call transcript (Q1 or Q2 FY2026) names a specific rival by name. As a result, two of the three profiles above (Ford, GM) are sourced to the Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export rather than to Tesla's own filings, and the single most consequential real-world competitor by volume — BYD — appears nowhere in this data pool at all and is sourced only to dated, unverified web trade press. A full FY2025 10-K with its Item 1A Competition discussion, plus a peer-comp export that itself included BYD, would resolve this gap and let the `moat` agent anchor its "earns more than peers" claim to filing-grade rather than web-grade evidence for the company's most important rival.

## business-model / 09_moat.md

_Source: `business-model/09_moat.md`_

# Moat — TSLA

## 1. Named Competitors

(Inherited from `08_competitive-map.md`, which itself flags that Tesla's own filings in this data pool never name a specific competitor — only a Part III-only Form 10-K/A is present, with no Item 1A Competition section, and neither in-pool earnings-call transcript names a rival by name [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2, §5].)

- **BYD Company Limited** (HKEX:1211 / SZSE:002594) — battery-electric and plug-in-hybrid passenger vehicles globally; the volume leader that overtook Tesla as the world's top BEV seller in calendar 2025 (2.26 million BEV units vs Tesla's 1.64 million); named only in dated, unverified web trade press, not in any Tesla filing [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2].
- **Ford Motor Company** (NYSE:F) — US/global light-vehicle manufacturer with a growing EV lineup (Mustang Mach-E, F-150 Lightning); LTM revenue 1.83x Tesla's, but LTM net-income margin is −3.2% (a net loss) [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2, citing Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export].
- **General Motors Company** (NYSE:GM) — US/global light-vehicle manufacturer (Chevrolet, Cadillac, GMC, Buick) with its own EV lineup and a large China joint-venture presence; LTM revenue 1.79x Tesla's, profitable at the operating line but well below Tesla on gross and net margin, and carrying far more balance-sheet leverage (67% debt/capital vs Tesla's 15.5%) [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2].

## 2. Moat Sources

| Possible Moat | Present? (Y/N) | Evidence | Strength /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Brand | Y | Tesla sells direct to consumer with no franchised-dealer markup and commands a P/Diluted-EPS multiple of 296x [Company Profile, Jul-23-2026] that no named peer approaches, evidence of a large intangible premium investors and buyers assign to the name; but the brand has not translated into pricing power — automotive average selling price moves have been "primarily driven by sales mix" and FX, not list-price increases, and gross margin fell for three straight years [`03_segment-map.md` §1; Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A, restated in `07_business-quality.md` row 1] | 40 |
| Cost advantage | N | Vertical integration into lithium refining and cathode/cell production is real [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A, "we started production with the lithium refinery, the cathode refinery... we're scaling up battery cell production"], but it has not shown up as a cost advantage that protects margin: automotive gross margin fell from 18.2% (FY2023) to 16.2% (FY2025) even with per-unit cost "relatively consistent" [`06_value-chain.md` §2], and Tesla's own LTM gross margin (18.9%) sits below GM (10.2%) only nominally higher, not below Ford/GM on a cost-per-unit basis that is disclosed anywhere in this pool | 25 |
| Distribution | Y | Owns its own stores, website, delivery network, and service centers — no independent franchised dealer sits between Tesla and the buyer, unlike Ford and GM's dealer networks [`02_business-identity.md` §1; `06_value-chain.md` §1]. This is a structural difference from both named legacy competitors, but it has not been shown to convert into superior realized pricing (see Brand row) | 45 |
| Scale | Y | LTM revenue of $103,619M is smaller than Ford's ($189,861M) and GM's ($185,528M) in dollar terms [`08_competitive-map.md` §2], but on a units/gigafactory-footprint basis Tesla runs five vehicle-and-battery plants across three continents (Fremont, Austin, Berlin, Shanghai, Nevada) plus a Megafactory under construction near Houston [`06_value-chain.md` §1] purpose-built for EVs, versus legacy OEMs retrofitting mixed ICE/EV lines. Capex guided "in excess of $25 billion in 2026" [Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] signals scale ambition, not yet a margin-visible scale advantage | 35 |
| Technology / IP | Y | Proprietary battery-cell/cathode/lithium-refining technology, the NACS charging standard adopted by rival automakers under commercial agreement to use Tesla's Superchargers, and FSD (Supervised) software with roughly 55% of North America Q2 FY2026 deliveries carrying a paid subscription [`06_value-chain.md` §1, citing Q2 FY2026 transcript]. A patent-and-developed-technology intangible asset is disclosed in the Q2 FY2026 10-Q but not sized as a competitive barrier [`Tesla_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Jul-23-2026), Notes`]. This is the most evidenced "Y" row, though its economic payoff (robotaxi, Optimus) carries no disclosed revenue line yet [`07_business-quality.md` row: Industry rate-of-change] | 50 |
| Licenses / regulation | N | Regulation is a headwind, not a moat: automotive regulatory-credit revenue (a near-pure-margin line) fell 67% year-on-year in Q2 FY2026 under U.S. government action, and robotaxi scale-up is gated by unresolved, state-by-state safety regulation with "no federal framework" [`10_external-dependency.md` §1]. No exclusive license or regulatory barrier protects Tesla from BYD, Ford, or GM entering the same markets | 10 |
| Network effects | Y (partial, narrow) | The Supercharger network, now opened to rival OEMs under NACS on Tesla's own commercial terms, and the FSD/Autopilot fleet-data flywheel are real network-style assets [`06_value-chain.md` §1], but neither is quantified in this pool (no disclosed Supercharger stall count, no disclosed FSD miles-driven or disengagement-rate data) — the mechanism is plausible, the magnitude is "Not proven from available data" | 30 |
| Switching costs | N | Vehicle purchase/lease is "a one-off retail purchase/lease, not a standing contract" [`07_business-quality.md` row: Customer stickiness, citing `05_customer-geography.md` §1]; no long-term customer contracts are disclosed for Automotive, and Energy's utility/commercial buyers have only isolated framework agreements [`05_customer-geography.md` §1]. FSD-subscription retention and Supercharger-network stickiness are plausible but unquantified | 20 |
| Natural resource access | N | Tesla is a price-taker on globally traded battery-grade lithium, nickel, steel, and aluminum, and discloses dependence on "single source suppliers" without naming or sizing them [`06_value-chain.md` §1, §2, citing Q2 FY2026 10-Q Notes]. In-house lithium refining reduces but does not eliminate this exposure — it is a cost-mitigation program, not owned resource access | 15 |
| Location advantage | N | Gigafactories sit in Texas, Nevada, California, Berlin, and Shanghai for logistics and local-content reasons, but no disclosed evidence (tax holiday value, unique site advantage) shows this location set is a durable, hard-to-replicate edge over competitors who can and do build competing plants in the same regions (e.g., GM's own China joint-venture presence [`08_competitive-map.md` §2]) | 15 |

## 3. Competitive Economics

| Company / Competitor | Gross Margin | EBIT Margin | Return on capital (ROIC) | Period | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Tesla (TSLA) | 18.9% | 4.1% | 2.75% (LTM, CIQ vendor definition) / 3.15%–3.74% (own computed, see §3 note below) | LTM Jun-30-2026 | Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics tab; `Tesla Inc NasdaqGS TSLA Financials_Annual.xls`, Ratios tab; own calculation below |
| Competitor A — BYD | Not disclosed in this pool (peer-comp export excludes BYD) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed (~4.0% net margin is a web-derived estimate, not audited [`08_competitive-map.md` §2]) | FY2025 | `08_competitive-map.md` §2, citing Web: goodcarbadcar.net, pub. 2026-04-03, unverified |
| Competitor B — Ford | 7.1% | 0.8% | Not disclosed (net-income margin −3.2%, LTM total debt/capital 81.0%) | LTM (filing date 2026-04-30) | Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics tab, restated from `08_competitive-map.md` §2 |
| Competitor C — General Motors | 10.2% | 5.5% | Not disclosed (net-income margin 1.05%, LTM total debt/capital 66.9%) | LTM (filing date 2026-07-21) | Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics tab, restated from `08_competitive-map.md` §2 |

**Own computed ROIC, cross-checked against the CIQ vendor figure.** The Capital IQ Ratios tab reports "Return on Capital %" of 2.94% (FY2025) and 2.745% (LTM Jun-30-2026) [`Tesla Inc NasdaqGS TSLA Financials_Annual.xls`, Ratios tab] — a vendor-computed figure whose internal tax assumption is not disclosed (back-solving implies something close to a flat ~35% rate, not Tesla's actual effective rate). Recomputing on a standard base — NOPAT = EBIT × (1 − normalized tax rate), ÷ average invested capital — using the **normalized structural tax rate of ~26%** (LTM effective rate 25.9%, FY2025 27.0%; both exclude the FY2023 anomaly, where Income Tax Expense was **−$5,001M**, a one-time $5.9bn deferred-tax valuation-allowance release that made the FY2023 "Effective Tax Rate %" line NM/negative and is not representative of Tesla's structural tax burden [`Tesla Inc NasdaqGS TSLA Financials_Annual.xls`, Income Statement tab, "Effective Tax Rate %" and "Total Deferred Taxes" rows]):

- **Net-of-cash (strict) basis:** invested capital = Total Debt + Total Equity − Cash & Equivalents, averaged Dec-31-2025 ($81,071M) and Jun-30-2026 ($88,380M) → average $84,726M [`Tesla Inc NasdaqGS TSLA Financials_Annual.xls`, Balance Sheet tab; `Financials_Quarterly.xls`, Balance Sheet tab]. NOPAT (LTM EBIT $4,278M × (1 − 0.259)) = $3,168M. **ROIC (net-of-cash) = 3.74%.**
- **Gross-capital (pre-cash-netting) basis, shown because Tesla is net-cash:** invested capital = Total Debt + Total Equity only, averaged over the same two dates → average $100,592M. **ROIC (gross-capital) = 3.15%.**

The computed figures (3.15%–3.74%) diverge modestly from the CIQ vendor figure (2.75%) — both point to the same conclusion, and the gap is flagged rather than averaged away. The more conservative of the two bases available (CIQ's own 2.75% headline, and the gross-capital 3.15% computed figure) is used for the economic-moat test below.

**Through-cycle read (required, not a single peak year).** Tesla's own CIQ-reported Return on Capital series: FY2021 10.52%, **FY2022 18.58% (cyclical peak** — pandemic-era supply shortage plus a near-monopoly EV position, not repeatable [`07_business-quality.md` §4]), FY2023 8.90%, FY2024 5.97%, FY2025 2.94%, LTM 2.75% [`Tesla Inc NasdaqGS TSLA Financials_Annual.xls`, Ratios tab]. The 5-year average (FY2021–FY2025) is **~9.4%**; including LTM, **~8.3%**. Even on this through-cycle basis — which is far more favorable to Tesla than the latest LTM figure — the return sits below the cost-of-capital estimate developed next.

**The economic moat test (required).**

> Return on capital **below** cost of capital: **~2.75%–3.7% ROIC** (LTM, CIQ vendor / own computed range) and **~8.3%–9.4% ROIC** (5-year through-cycle average) vs **~11.5% WACC** (gap of roughly **770–885 basis points** on the LTM read, and **~210–320 basis points** even on the more favorable through-cycle average) — [Tesla Inc NasdaqGS TSLA Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab; own NOPAT/invested-capital calculation above; WACC is a CAPM estimate, **Inference, not from filings**, basis below].

**Cost-of-capital basis (no company-disclosed WACC or hurdle rate exists in this pool).** Tesla does not state a cost of equity, WACC, or hurdle rate anywhere in the filings or transcripts in this data pool — this is a CAPM estimate, clearly labelled inference: cost of equity = risk-free rate (~4.3%, approximate 10-year US Treasury yield, mid-2026) + beta (1.80, the disclosed 5-year beta [`Tesla-Inc-NasdaqGS-TSLA-Public-Company-Profile.txt`; Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics tab]) × equity-risk-premium (~5.0%, a standard long-run US estimate) ≈ **13.3%**. Pre-tax cost of debt ≈ interest expense ÷ average total debt (LTM $334M ÷ ~$15,400M ≈ 2.2%; Tesla's disclosed debt carries unusually low coupons relative to its rating, a fact not independently explained in this pool), after-tax at the 25.9% normalized rate ≈ 1.6%. Weighting at the LTM debt/capital mix (15.5% debt / 84.5% equity [`Tesla Inc NasdaqGS TSLA Financials_Annual.xls`, Ratios tab, "Total Debt/Capital %"]): **WACC ≈ 11.5%.** *Inference, not from filings.*

## 4. Where The Company Sits

1. **Relative to peers.** Tesla sits at the **top** of the three named competitors on gross margin (18.9% vs Ford's 7.1% and GM's 10.2%) [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics tab] but the **bottom** among the profitable pair on EBIT margin trend direction — Tesla's EBIT margin has fallen every year for three straight years (16.8% FY2022 → 4.6% FY2025 → 4.1% LTM [`07_business-quality.md` row: Margin stability]) while GM's LTM EBIT margin (5.5%) currently exceeds Tesla's (4.1%) in absolute terms despite GM's much lower gross margin. BYD's return-on-capital cannot be compared at all — not disclosed anywhere in this pool, only a web-derived, unverified net-margin estimate exists [`08_competitive-map.md` §2].
2. **Absolute (the economic moat test).** The company earns a return on capital **below** its cost of capital: **~2.75%–3.7%** LTM (and **~8.3%–9.4%** even on the more favorable 5-year through-cycle average) **vs ~11.5%** estimated WACC — the decisive test that any structural advantage identified in §2 has not translated into economic value creation.

## 5. Moat Verdict

**No moat proven.**

The strongest candidate is **Technology / IP** (strength 50/100) — proprietary battery-cell/lithium-refining vertical integration, the NACS charging standard now licensed to rival OEMs, and a paid FSD-subscription attach rate near 55% of North America deliveries [`06_value-chain.md` §1] — followed by Distribution (45/100, direct-to-consumer with no dealer network) and Brand (40/100, evidenced by the equity multiple, not by pricing power). But **CLAUDE.md's hard rule applies**: return on capital sits below cost of capital on every basis computed here — LTM (2.75%–3.7% vs ~11.5% WACC) and even the more forgiving 5-year through-cycle average (8.3%–9.4% vs ~11.5% WACC) — so no combination of these structural advantages can be scored a Strong or even a middling Narrow moat; this is a **moat in structure, not economics**: real scale, distribution, and technology assets that have not lifted the return on capital to or above what raising that capital costs. Durability over the next 5 years would need proof that automotive gross margin (16.2% FY2025, falling every year [`07_business-quality.md` row: Margin stability]) stabilizes as the shrinking regulatory-credit line fully runs off, and that FSD/robotaxi/Optimus — still a zero-disclosed-revenue-line item — converts a technology asset into a return-on-capital improvement rather than a growing capital drag; per `07_business-quality.md`'s "fast-changing industry" flag (rate-of-change score 30, ≤40), any such durability claim is discounted further because the winners in EV, battery-chemistry, and autonomous-driving competition are not knowable in advance (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 5).

**Moat trajectory — eroding.** Return on capital has fallen every year for three straight years and the gap to cost of capital has widened, not narrowed: from **above** WACC in FY2021–FY2022 (10.5%–18.6% vs ~11.5% WACC) to materially **below** WACC every year since (8.9% FY2023, 6.0% FY2024, 2.9% FY2025, 2.75% LTM) [`Tesla Inc NasdaqGS TSLA Financials_Annual.xls`, Ratios tab]. Pricing power is falling in parallel — automotive gross margin fell every year FY2023–FY2025 with management crediting only mix, FX, and a shrinking regulatory-credit line, not sticker-price increases, for holding margin up at all [`06_value-chain.md` §3] — and global BEV volume share was lost to BYD on a full calendar-year-2025 basis (Tesla 8.8% vs BYD 12.1% [`08_competitive-map.md` §3]). Entry/disruption pressure is rising, not falling, per `07_business-quality.md`'s Competitive intensity (28/100) and rate-of-change (30/100) rows. The one genuine counter-signal — automotive-sales revenue up 23–27% year-on-year in Q1–Q2 FY2026 after a Q4 FY2025 decline [`08_competitive-map.md` §3] — is a volume rebound, not evidence the margin or capital-return trend has turned; it does not change the trajectory call.

## business-model / 10_external-dependency.md

_Source: `business-model/10_external-dependency.md`_

# External Dependency Check — TSLA

## 1. Dependency Table

| External Variable | Dependency Level (Low / Mid / High) | Why It Matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commodity prices | Mid | Battery-cell inputs (lithium, nickel, cobalt) and steel/aluminum feed directly into cost of automotive and energy-storage sales. Management flags this as a live, current cost pressure, not a hedged-away one. | "Commodity price increases and interest rate changes all continue to add to our costs" [Q2 FY26 transcript, prepared remarks]; raw materials inventory of $4.70bn at Jun-30-2026 vs $4.52bn at Dec-31-2025 [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Note — Inventory] |
| Interest rates | High | Tesla subsidizes below-market loan/lease rates for buyers ("subvention"); the cost of that subsidy is booked upfront against automotive revenue, so rising rates cut margin directly, and higher rates also raise monthly payments for buyers financing a $40k+ vehicle, hitting demand. | "Interest rate subvention costs are recognized upfront as revenue offset. So, as interest rates have risen this year, the cost of subvention has risen along with them, which had a negative impact on automotive margins" [Q2 FY26 transcript, prepared remarks]; "central banks in developed countries raised interest rates rapidly and substantially, which impacted the affordability of vehicle lease and finance arrangements" [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] |
| FX | Mid | Roughly half of revenue is booked outside the US (see geography evidence below), mainly in Chinese yuan and euro, and the company does not hedge. A single-quarter FX swing has moved automotive average selling price and cost of sales in both directions. | "We ... have foreign currency risks related to our revenue, costs of revenue and operating expenses denominated in currencies other than the U.S. dollar (primarily the Chinese yuan and euro)... we do not typically hedge foreign currency risk" [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Item 3]; a 10% adverse move across all currencies would swing pre-tax income by $1.64bn at Jun-30-2026 (see §2) [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Item 3]; International revenue (China $20,962mn + Other International $26,238mn) = $47,200mn of $94,827mn total FY25 revenue, ~50% [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments tab, FY2025] |
| Freight / logistics rates | Not separately disclosed as a distinct sensitivity — folded into the broader "supply chain cost structure" risk language under tariffs/trade policy below. Skipped as its own row; no standalone dependency level can be assigned without double-counting the tariff row. | — | — |
| Government policy | High | Two separate policy levers hit results directly: (1) federal/state automotive regulatory-credit programs, which are a nearly pure-margin revenue line now being rolled back, and (2) the OBBBA and tariff regime, which management says materially raises battery-cell costs for the energy business. | "Automotive regulatory credits revenue decreased $293 million, or 67%, in the three months ended June 30, 2026... Recent governmental and regulatory actions have restricted certain regulatory credit programs tied to our products" [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A]; "import tariffs by the US government and the provisions of the OBBBA could significantly increase battery cell expenses and impact costs for our consumers, negatively impacting consumer demand" [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] |
| Regulation | High | Two distinct regulatory dependencies beyond the credits above: vehicle/robotaxi safety regulation (state-by-state, evolving sensor-requirement rules) gates the scale-up of the robotaxi and FSD business the company is now pricing into its story, and a February 2026 Supreme Court ruling on IEEPA tariffs shows outcomes can swing on litigation Tesla does not control. | "There seems to be some evolving regulations at the state level, potentially around sensor requirements... TCO transportation regulatory situations are different city by city, state by state — there is not a federal framework" [Q2 FY26 transcript, Q&A, Lars Moravy]; "the U.S. Supreme Court issued a ruling invalidating certain tariffs previously imposed under [IEEPA]. As a result... we may be eligible for a refund" [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] |
| Weather | Not material as a standalone disclosed sensitivity for a global multi-factory manufacturer; skipped rather than defaulted to Low. | — | — |
| Geopolitics | Mid | China is ~22% of FY2025 revenue and hosts a Gigafactory; the tariff/trade-policy language spans US-China and broader trade-policy uncertainty, and management explicitly ties near-term risk to "rapidly evolving trade and fiscal policy and geopolitical conflicts." | "As a result of rapidly evolving trade and fiscal policy and geopolitical conflicts, uncertainty in the automotive and energy markets continues, posing risks to our global supply chain and cost structure" [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A]; China revenue $20,962mn of $94,827mn total FY25 revenue, ~22% [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments tab, FY2025] |
| Consumer cycle | High | Automotive is ~86.5% of FY2025 revenue ($82,056mn of $94,827mn) and management explicitly ties order rates and margin to "shifting consumer trends," inflation, energy prices, and interest-rate-driven affordability — none of which Tesla sets. | Automotive $82,056mn / Total $94,827mn, FY2025 [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments tab]; "we operate in a cyclical industry that is sensitive to shifting consumer trends, geopolitical conflicts, political and regulatory uncertainty... all of which can be compounded by inflationary pressures, rising energy prices, interest rate fluctuations... These macroeconomic and industry trends have had, and will likely continue to have, an impact on the pricing of, and order rate for our vehicles, and in turn our operating margin" [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] |
| Industrial cycle | Mid | The energy-storage (Megapack) business is lumpy because deployments track customer construction and grid-interconnect timelines — largely data-center/grid-buildout capex cycles Tesla does not control — even though the segment is only ~13.5% of FY2025 revenue. | "Energy business is inherently lumpy. Deployments are tied to customer time lines and largely out of our control" [Q2 FY26 transcript, prepared remarks]; Energy Generation and Storage revenue $12,771mn of $94,827mn total FY2025 revenue, ~13.5% [CIQ Financials_Annual export, Segments tab, FY2025] |

## 2. Sensitivity, If Disclosed

| Variable | Disclosed Sensitivity | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| FX (all currencies, 10% adverse move) | Would swing net income before income taxes by a gain or loss of $1.64bn (measured Jun-30-2026) vs. $1.70bn (measured Dec-31-2025) — applied to total monetary assets/liabilities in non-local currencies, assuming no hedging | Q2 FY26 10-Q, Item 3 (Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk) |

No interest-rate or commodity-price sensitivity table is disclosed in Item 3 of the Q2 FY26 10-Q (that section covers FX only) — the interest-rate and commodity cost impact above is described qualitatively in the MD&A and earnings call, not quantified in a formal sensitivity table. This is a gap: "Not proven from available data" for a numeric interest-rate or commodity beta on margin.

## 3. Classification

**Partly externally driven.** Tesla is not a pure external-variable pass-through — pricing, vertical integration (in-house battery/cathode/lithium-refining capacity), cost-reduction programs, and product mix are real, demonstrated management levers, and the company explicitly credits these for holding automotive margin "approximately flat" ex one-off items in Q2 FY26 [Q2 FY26 transcript, prepared remarks]. But the exposure is material and only partly hedgeable: regulatory-credit revenue (a nearly pure-margin line) has been cut by government action outside Tesla's control (-67% YoY in Q2 FY26), interest-rate subvention costs move automatically with rate policy, roughly half of revenue sits in unhedged foreign currency, and the newer growth narratives (robotaxi, FSD, Megapack) are each gated by a regulator or a customer's own capex timeline rather than by Tesla's execution alone.

## 4. External Dependency Risk Score

**58/100** (inverted: higher = worse)

Rationale: the automotive core (~86.5% of FY2025 revenue) sits inside a self-acknowledged cyclical, rate-sensitive, policy-sensitive industry, and the regulatory-credit line — which is effectively a government subsidy dressed as revenue — has already been cut by more than half year-on-year under current policy. That combination (consumer-cycle + rate + policy exposure, all in the same segment) pushes the score above the "mixed" midpoint. It stays below the 61+ ("mostly externally driven") band because Tesla retains real, evidenced levers — vertical integration into lithium refining and cell manufacturing, pricing/mix management that held margin flat ex one-offs, and a service/software (FSD subscription) revenue stream that is not commodity- or rate-linked in the same way.

## 5. The Single Biggest Lever

A sustained further rollback of automotive regulatory-credit programs and EV/energy purchase incentives — a policy variable already cutting Q2 FY26 credit revenue by 67% YoY [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Item 2 MD&A] — would do the most damage if it moved another 20% adverse, because that revenue drops to the bottom line at close to 100% margin and the company has no substitute lever to replace it in the short run.

## 1. Signal Table

| Dividend policy & coverage | Tesla has paid $0 in dividends every year since at least 2017 and pairs that with zero buybacks, so all cash generated is retained rather than returned to shareholders — a stated growth-stage policy rather than a coverage problem, since operating cash flow ($18,685M LTM) comfortably exceeds capex ($12,923M LTM). | [Capital IQ export, Financials_Annual — Cash Flow tab, "Total Dividends Paid" row, FY2017–LTM Jun-2026] | 20 |
| Capex intensity vs depreciation (growth vs maintenance) | Capex has run 1.4x–2.2x depreciation & amortization every year since 2021 (FY2025: $8,527M capex vs $6,148M D&A = 1.39x; LTM Jun-2026: $12,923M vs $6,477M = 2.00x) even as FY2025 revenue fell 2.9% from FY2024 ($94,827M vs $97,690M) and operating margin compressed from 7.8% to 4.6% — capex is rising on unproven AI/robotics/compute bets while the core auto business shrinks. | [Capital IQ export, Financials_Annual — Cash Flow tab, "Capital Expenditure" and "Depreciation & Amort., Total" rows; Capital IQ export, Financials_Annual — Income Statement tab, "Total Revenue" and "Operating Income" rows, FY2024–FY2025] | 55 |
| Debt level and trajectory (absolute + vs EBITDA) | Total debt is modest and net cash is large and growing: Total Debt/EBITDA is 1.64x LTM (up from 0.32x in FY2022 as EBITDA compressed) but net debt (strict basis: total debt minus cash & short-term investments) is a negative $27.4 billion (net cash) as of Jun-2026, up from negative $22.9 billion at FY2025-end. | [Capital IQ export, Financials_Annual — Capital Structure Summary tab, "Total Debt/EBITDA" and "Net Debt" rows, FY2022–LTM Jun-2026; Capital IQ export, Financials_Annual — Balance Sheet tab, "Total Debt" and "Net Debt" rows] | 15 |

| Insider / promoter ownership and changes | CEO Elon Musk holds 1,123.3 million shares (29.91% of shares outstanding, $420.1 billion market value) as of Jun-16-2026, a stake that has been preserved rather than diluted through successive performance-award grants that add new shares disproportionately to his own holding, while total institutional ownership sits at 41.71%. | [Capital IQ export, Public Ownership Summary, "Top Holders" table, position date Jun-16-2026] | 35 |
| Promoter share pledging *(if applicable, e.g. Indian listings)* | Applicable — Board policy caps CEO pledging-collateralized borrowing at the lesser of $3.5 billion or 25% of the pledged stock's value (15% for other directors/officers), and the CEO's beneficial-ownership footnote discloses 207.5 million shares "eligible to be pledged" as collateral for personal indebtedness, but the company states that as of Dec-31-2025 the aggregate loan amount collateralized by all directors' and officers' pledged shares was under 1% of the pledged shares' value — far below the 50% threshold that would be a hard disqualifier. | [FY2025 10-K/A (Apr-30-2026), "Pledging of Shares" policy, p.11380-11484; beneficial ownership footnote, p.12548] | 30 |
| Auditor history (changes, qualifications, key audit matters) | PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP remains the auditor with no disclosed change, resignation, or dismissal, and its consent is filed with the FY2025 annual report; no qualified opinion or going-concern language appears anywhere in the pool. | [FY2025 10-K/A (Apr-30-2026), p.832 and p.16745, "Consent of PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP"] | 10 |
| Restatements / accounting policy changes | The Capital IQ workbook tags Dec-2018 and Dec-2021 balance-sheet columns "Restated," but this is Capital IQ's own multi-year data-conformity label, not a disclosed SEC-mandated restatement by Tesla found anywhere in the pool — whether it reflects an actual company restatement is not proven from available data. | [Capital IQ export, Financials_Annual — Balance Sheet tab, column headers "Restated Dec-31-2018" / "Restated Dec-31-2021"] | 15 |
| Off-balance-sheet items | Maximum exposure on vehicle resale-value guarantees to leasing-bank partners rose to $4.07 billion (Jun-2026) from $3.45 billion (Dec-2025) while the recorded guarantee liability is described only as "immaterial," and a jury verdict against Tesla of $329 million combined compensatory and punitive damages (Benavides v. Tesla, Aug-2025) is on appeal with only an "immaterial accrual" booked against it. | [Q2 2026 10-Q (Jul-23-2026), Note on guarantees, p.6769-6786; Commitments and Contingencies, "Benavides v. Tesla, Inc.", p.12339 area] | 40 |
| Working capital trend (receivable days, inventory days, cash conversion) | The cash conversion cycle has deteriorated from -12.1 days (FY2021, meaning suppliers financed operations) to +14.0 days (FY2025) and +13.0 days (LTM Jun-2026), driven mainly by inventory days rising from 44.7 (FY2021) to 61.5 (LTM), while days-sales-outstanding stayed low (14.0 LTM). | [Capital IQ export, Financials_Annual — Ratios tab, "Avg. Days Sales Out.", "Avg. Days Inventory Out.", "Avg. Cash Conversion Cycle" rows, FY2021–LTM Jun-2026] | 30 |
| Senior management turnover (CEO, CFO, board chair in last 3 years) | The CEO (since Oct-2008) and Board Chair Robyn Denholm (chair since 2018) have no turnover; the CFO changed once, in August 2023 (Vaibhav Taneja replacing Zachary Kirkhorn), which falls just inside a trailing-3-year window from Jul-2026 but is otherwise the only senior-management change disclosed. | [FY2025 10-K/A (Apr-30-2026), Executive Officer bios, p.2382-2388; Audit Committee composition, p.2239-2241] | 25 |

**Acquisition pattern — serial-acquirer + opportunity-cost test (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 4).** Tesla shows no serial-acquirer pattern: cash acquisitions were $0 in five of the last six fiscal years and never debt-funded or large relative to the company's own value [Capital IQ export, Financials_Annual — Cash Flow tab]. The one capital commitment that resembles deal activity — the $2.0 billion equity stake in SpaceX/xAI Holdings — is a related-party investment in an entity the CEO controls, not an operating acquisition, and is scored under the related-party-transactions row rather than here. No rejector-filter cap applies from this row.

## 2. Classification

**Governance red flags.**

The signal profile is dominated by how the company is run rather than by how its cash is spent in the ordinary sense: a sprawling network of transactions and capital commitments with the CEO's other controlled entities (SpaceX, xAI, The Boring Company), Delaware derivative litigation alleging breach of fiduciary duty tied to those same relationships, a $132.3 billion maximum-value CEO performance award that dilutes public shareholders while a voting agreement and prior award design have preserved the CEO's own economic and voting position, and a disclosed pattern of booking only "immaterial" reserves against an actual $329 million adverse jury verdict. None of these individually clears the disqualifier-scan's hard triggers (no audit qualification, no going concern, pledging utilization under 1% of collateral value, related-party revenue an immaterial share of total revenue), but together they describe a company whose governance structure concentrates outsized, contingent economic power in one individual with extensive outside interests.

## 3. Most Material Signal

The net share count trajectory — specifically the 2025 CEO Performance Award — is the signal that would most change this classification if it worsens further. The award grants up to 423.7 million shares (about 10.7% of shares outstanding at grant) with a maximum grant-date fair value of $132.3 billion [FY2025 10-K/A, p.5192, p.4168], vesting in 12 tranches tied to market-capitalization milestones from $2.0 trillion to reportedly much higher levels. If additional tranches are certified as earned, or if a similar follow-on award is granted before this one is even fully earned (as happened with the 2018 award), the dilution to public shareholders' economic claim on the company would compound further while the CEO's own percentage ownership and control are structurally protected — this is the one lever that could turn "governance red flags" into a harder disqualifier-level concern.

## 4. Capital Allocation Score /100

**62/100.**

No rejector-filter cap applies: the acquisition-pattern row scored 20/100 severity, well below the 70-severity threshold that would trigger the Filter-4 cap under CLAUDE.md §24 and MODULE_RULES.md. The score instead reflects a weighted read of the table — heavy weight on the net share count trajectory (70 severity) and the related-party transaction network (55 severity) as the two most consequential rows, moderate weight on capex intensity (55) and off-balance-sheet items (40), and a large offsetting credit for the balance sheet itself: near-zero absolute debt, a $27.4 billion net cash position, a clean and unchanged auditor, and no evidence of a genuine restatement.

## 3. Most Severe New Flag

The unresolved securities-fraud class action naming Tesla, Elon Musk, and named executives personally over alleged misrepresentations of Autopilot, FSD (Supervised), and Robotaxi effectiveness is the most material new flag. It is not a background legal-inquiry item — it is an active federal case with the motion-to-dismiss still pending, filed against the exact narrative (autonomous driving and robotaxi economics) that `business-quality` already identified as Tesla's main forward bet and the reason it capped the business as a sector/technology-cycle wager rather than a durable compounder. A ruling that lets the case proceed would put a securities-fraud discovery process directly on top of the same claims the market is pricing into Tesla's multi-trillion-dollar robotaxi-driven valuation narrative, and it comes bundled with two related, separately-filed consumer class actions over the same underlying driver-assistance claims. The synthesizer should treat this as a distinct, evidenced litigation overhang on the specific technology the bull case depends on — separate from, and additive to, the product-liability verdict and derivative suits `capital-allocation-governance` already flagged.

## 4. Cross-Cutting Patterns

Four independent data points — the failed 2025 bylaw reform (supermajority voting and the 3% derivative-suit threshold both retained), the succession framework gated to the two most speculative pay-package tranches and self-authored by the CEO, the reported SpaceX/xAI merger discussions, and the already-flagged $132.3bn pay package and SpaceX/xAI related-party dealings — point the same direction: every recent governance decision point available in this data pool has widened, not narrowed, the concentration of unchecked economic and legal power in one individual, at the same time minority shareholders' structural tools to challenge that concentration (the derivative-suit threshold, supermajority protections) were left in place rather than reformed. Separately, the securities and consumer class actions over Autopilot/FSD/Robotaxi claims are not free-standing legal noise — they attack the specific narrative (autonomous driving, robotaxi) that `business-quality` and `external-dependency` both already flagged as unproven and central to how the market values the stock, so a discovery process or an adverse ruling in that litigation is one of the few events that could simultaneously damage the legal, reputational, and valuation cases at once.
